title: "Figure 4—figure supplement (number pending) — can the distortion be undone by counting fewer intervals? The SIZE of the information distortion against its SHAPE"

<!--
NUMBER PENDING, as for the other rebuilt supplements.

THE QUESTION, and it is the one a reader reaches for the moment Figure 4 shows a distortion. If the
likelihood overstates its information, can that be repaired by declaring that the recording holds
fewer independent intervals than it appears to? That repair is the standard one, it costs nothing,
and the lag supplement already measures the number it would use. It works if and only if the
distortion is a SCALAR: every parameter direction wrong by the same factor. This figure measures
whether it is.

WHAT IT IS. Two panels over the same plane, six members, one column each, 12 columns. Both read
GIDM, the same matrix Figure 4's B half draws one diagonal entry of, and both are invariants of its
whole spectrum:

  A  magnitude    exp(mean(log lambda_i)) = det(GIDM)^(1/p), the geometric mean of the eigenvalues.
                  The typical factor by which the reported information is wrong, over all
                  directions at once. Null 1, and SIGNED: below 1 the member understates what it
                  knows, above 1 it overstates it.
  B  anisotropy   exp(sd(log lambda_i)), how much that factor VARIES from direction to direction,
                  read as a spread: the per-direction ratios sit within a factor of this either
                  side of the magnitude. Null 1, and one-sided, since a spread cannot be negative.

WHY THEY ARE THE RIGHT PAIR and not two arbitrary summaries: they are the orthogonal components of
a quantity the set already reports, exactly, with p = 6 the number of parameters,

    affine_invariant_distance^2 = p * (mean(log lambda))^2 + p * (sd(log lambda))^2

so panel A is the whole distortion that a scalar correction COULD absorb and panel B is the whole
of what it could not. Panel B at 1 means an effective-N rescaling is exact, and the factor it should
use is panel A. Panel B above 1 means no such rescaling exists at any factor, whatever the lag
supplement reports. That is the entire argument, and it is why the two panels belong on one page.

Verified against the emitted spectrum, 2026-08-02, INR at N_ch 1e4 / noise 0.1 / interval 0.01:
log_Det 18.63817 = 6 * 3.106361, and 6 * (3.106361^2 + 4.868375) = 87.107 = 9.333113^2. The emitted
logs are natural and the emitted variance divides by p, not by p - 1.

ONE SCALE AND ONE BAR, which is the point of drawing them together. Both are factors on an
information ratio with a null of 1, which is the same kind of number as Figure 4's B half and is
read against the same two criteria, 1.15 and 2. So they take SCALE_FACTOR, the set's default, and
`fig4_render` gives them a single bar across the width. A colour here means what it means in
Figure 4. The anisotropy occupies only the upper arm, since it cannot fall below 1; that is half a
diverging scale unused, and it is bought deliberately, because the comparison this figure exists to
make is A against B cell for cell and a second bar would break it. Every other one-sided quantity in
this set (the standard error, the autocorrelation time, the condition number) is drawn alone or
against something incommensurable, and takes a sequential scale for exactly the reason that does not
apply here.

WHAT IT SHOWS. Medians over the seven intervals at noise 0.1, pool anchor, as factors:

                     N_ch:     10       100      1000     10000
    magnitude       ILSE       5.79     6.10     6.15     6.08
                    NR         6.68    15.07    30.13    99.37
                    INR        5.16     5.01     4.94     4.93
                    R          1.09     1.15     1.23     1.24
                    MR         1.30     1.46     1.51     1.56
                    IR         1.02     1.00     1.00     1.00
    anisotropy      ILSE       3.17     3.20     3.17     3.22
                    NR         3.90     5.99    15.32    86.15
                    INR        3.18     3.26     3.28     3.30
                    R          1.29     1.17     1.18     1.19
                    MR         1.40     1.36     1.38     1.39
                    IR         1.25     1.15     1.07     1.04

THE ANSWER IS NO, and it is not close. Wherever the magnitude is large the anisotropy is large with
it: least squares and the open-loop interval member each overstate their information by about a
factor 5 to 6, and the per-direction factor spreads by 3.2 around that, so directions exist that are
wrong by 20 and directions exist that are barely wrong at all. A single effective count cannot serve
both. The claim the reader would otherwise make, that the integrated autocorrelation of the residual
gives the correction, is refuted on the same page that would have supplied the number.

ILSE AND INR ARE FLAT IN THE CHANNEL COUNT and nearly equal to each other, 6.1 against 4.9 in
magnitude and 3.2 against 3.3 in shape. Neither tracks the temporal correlation, and what they lose
by not tracking it does not depend on how many channels there are. NR, which does not track it
either but keeps the sample-level variance, is the one that runs away: 99 and 86 at ten thousand,
where the anisotropy has almost caught the magnitude.

THE THREE RECURSIVE MEMBERS SEPARATE ON DIFFERENT AXES, which is worth a sentence in the caption.
R's magnitude DRIFTS UP with the channel count, 1.09 to 1.24, while its shape sits flat at about
1.18: its failure is mostly a size it could in principle correct for. IR's magnitude is already 1 at
every count and its anisotropy FALLS, 1.25 to 1.04, so it is the only member converging on both axes
at once. IR at ten channels is the honest exception in this figure: 1.25 is above the strict
criterion, so even the boundary-conditioned filter is not isotropic when there are ten channels to
filter.

MR IS WORSE THAN THE MEMBER IT IMPROVES ON, on both axes and at every channel count: 1.30 to 1.56 in
size against R's 1.09 to 1.24, and 1.36 to 1.40 in shape against R's flat 1.18. It carries the
interval treatment R does not have and costs more for it, and it is further from honest than R is.
That is the ladder claim in its sharpest form, and it is a claim this figure makes and the bias half
of Figure 4 cannot: a partial interval correction does not interpolate between the member without
one and the member with a complete one, it is off the ladder altogether. Whether VR behaves the same
way is one line in the roster and one recalibration to 14 columns, both already measured.

THE NOISE FLOOR, and it is the reason both panels are CI-aware. Both statistics are biased AWAY from
their null by estimation noise alone: a spectrum estimated from a finite bootstrap spreads even when
the truth is isotropic, so a raw anisotropy is never exactly 1 and the panel would show structure
where there is none. Each cell is therefore drawn at the EDGE of its 95 per cent interval toward the
null, the same collapse `Dconf` uses, so a cell whose interval brackets 1 renders white. IR's 1.04
at ten thousand channels is the cell to watch: if it survives the collapse it is a real residual
anisotropy, and if it goes white the floor is where it should be. That reading belongs in the
caption either way, since it is what calibrates every other number on the page.

THE ROSTER, and why MR is in it. The organising axis is the instantaneous/interval pairing at each
level of the stochasticity ladder, which wants LSE and ILSE, NR and INR, R and IR. The un-averaged
least squares (av = 0) has no run yet, so that column is a gap, and MR takes the sixth place until
it lands. Two reasons, and the second is the one that decided it. MR is the partially-corrected
interval member, so it belongs on the axis this figure draws and it turns out to carry the sharpest
version of the ladder claim (above). And the page is what sets the column count: at five members the
figure is 9.15 in tall against a 9.263 in text height, which leaves 0.11 in for a legend and does
not fit. A column ADDED makes it shorter, since the cell narrows and a square cell then wants less
height, so the sixth member is what puts the figure on the page at all. The arithmetic is in the
render chunk.

The member the rest of the set labels LSE is the AVERAGED one, av = 1, and it is labelled ILSE here
because this figure is organised by exactly that distinction and calling it LSE would break the axis
the figure is about. That relabel is pending across the rest of the set.

VR IS NOT HERE, and it is the only member left out. Adding it is one line in the roster and one
number in the render chunk, 14 columns at per_row 0.2128 and 6.65 in, already measured. It is out
today only because six members is what the page wanted and MR was the more informative sixth.
-->

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
```

```{r common, include=FALSE}
# The ladder, in order, paired: no stochasticity, sample variance, recursion, each in its
# instantaneous and its interval form. ../data/0ffbda7 carries the averaged least squares and
# ../data/1f7138b carries INR; neither supplies anything the frozen dirs already have.
FIG4_ALGOS     <- c("nonlinearsqr", "macro_NR", "macro_INR", "macro_R", "macro_MR", "macro_IR")
FIG4_ALGO_LAB  <- c(nonlinearsqr = "ILSE", macro_NR = "NR", macro_INR = "INR",
                    macro_R = "R", macro_MR = "MR", macro_IR = "IR")
FIG4_DATA_DIRS <- c("../data/1c2ae6f", "../data/87889e6", "../data/0ffbda7", "../data/1f7138b")
# The inner level is the QUANTITY, as in the lag/kappa supplement: neither has a parameter index,
# so each member costs one column per side and the strip names what is in it.
FIG4_PARS   <- c("mag", "aniso")
FIG4_PSHORT <- c(mag = "size", aniso = "shape")
source("figure_4_common.R")
source("figure_4_layout.R")
```

```{r sides}
# Both halves come out of the shared source data (figure_4_data.R), already as factors with a null
# of 1, so this notebook reads five small CSVs and no battery file. NEITHER side declares a scale:
# they are commensurable by construction, so both take SCALE_FACTOR and fig4_render gives them one
# bar across the width, which is what lets them be compared rather than merely juxtaposed.
spec <- dplyr::filter(.fig4_src$spec, algo %in% ALGOS, is.finite(Sconf), Sconf > 0)

SIDES <- list(
  list(lab = "size of the information distortion", letter = "A",
       data = dplyr::filter(spec, param == "mag"),   zf = function(x) log10(x$Sconf)),
  list(lab = "shape: spread across directions", letter = "B",
       data = dplyr::filter(spec, param == "aniso"), zf = function(x) log10(x$Sconf)))
```

```{r render, fig.width = 7.4, fig.height = 7.69}
# 12 columns over two sides, no key row and no white contours: a standard error is not defined for a
# quantity with no parameter index. per_row 0.2512, x 0.2289, y 0.2289, 100.0 per cent
# (tmp/calib_fig4.R case 12T2), cell 1.66 mm.
#
# THE COLUMN COUNT IS SET BY THE PAGE, and the direction is the opposite of the obvious one: a
# column ADDED makes this figure SHORTER, because the height follows from the cell being square and
# the cell narrows as columns are added. Measured from the class this manuscript uses (9pt elife,
# letterpaper): \textheight is 666.93 pt = 9.263 in and a fullwidth \linewidth is 534.63 pt =
# 7.425 in, so a 7.40 in PDF lands essentially 1:1 and the whole height budget for a figure AND its
# legend is 9.263 in. The three rosters, all measured:
#   10 columns, five members     per_row 0.3049, 9.15 in, cell 2.05 mm  DOES NOT FIT: 0.11 in left
#                                                                       for a legend
#   12 columns, six members      per_row 0.2512, 7.69 in, cell 1.66 mm  fits, 1.57 in for the legend
#   14 columns, all seven        per_row 0.2128, 6.65 in, cell 1.38 mm  fits, 2.61 in, and lands on
#                                                                       the lag/kappa geometry
# Twelve is the one drawn. Fourteen is seven members, so it covers EITHER the un-averaged least
# squares landing OR VR joining, not both: the two together are sixteen columns and are not
# measured, and at that width the cell is under 1.4 mm and the roster wants a second look anyway.
fig4_render(SIDES, per_row = 0.2512, out = "Figure_4_supplement_magnitude_anisotropy.pdf",
            se_lines = FALSE, key = FALSE)
```

```{r table}
# The medians in the note, rebuilt from the source data so the note cannot drift from the figure.
# `m` and not `Sconf`: the CI edge is the right value for a MAP and the wrong one for a printed
# number, where it would report the edge of an interval as though it were the estimate.
spec %>%
  dplyr::filter(abs(ly - log10(0.1)) < 1e-9) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(param, algo, Num_ch) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(v = median(m), .groups = "drop") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(algo = factor(ALGO_LAB[algo], levels = ALGO_LAB[ALGOS]),
                param = factor(param, levels = c("mag", "aniso"))) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = Num_ch, values_from = v) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(param, algo) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  print(digits = 3)
```
